In Portugal, temperatures could approach 38°C in the Alentejo and the Tagus Valley, driven by an anticyclone positioned to the north of the Azores.
Portugal is set to experience a gradual rise in temperatures from this Saturday, with weather conditions hotter than usual for this time of year. The warning comes from the Portuguese Institute for Sea and Atmosphere (IPMA) (source in Portuguese), which is even pointing to the likelihood of a heatwave.

"This spell of hot weather will be defined mainly by how long it lasts, with a high probability that it will develop into a heatwave across much of the country," the IPMA said in a statement.
The document explains that a heatwave occurs when, "over a period of six consecutive days, the maximum air temperature is 5 °C above the average value of the daily maximum temperatures".
Temperatures are therefore expected to reach above 30 °C in mainland Portugal. In some areas, such as Lisbon and the Tagus valley, they could even approach 38 °C.
Minimum temperatures will also rise, staying above 20 °C in some parts of Alto Alentejo, Beira Baixa, the Tagus valley and the eastern Algarve.
"Although the forecast maximum temperatures are lower than those recorded during some episodes this summer, they will be substantially higher than the average for the second half of September," the statement adds.
The hot weather is due to the "influence of an anticyclone located to the north of the Azores, extending in a ridge as far as the Bay of Biscay". This system will transport "a mass of continental air (hot and dry) over the Iberian Peninsula".
In July, Portugal had already recorded anomalous temperatures, with red warnings in most of the country and the government declaring a state of alert. The same situation extended to the rest of mainland Europe during the month of July.
A report by the non-profit organisation Climate Central concluded that the continent had been "the most abnormally warm region on the planet". Almost nine in ten Europeans lived through an entire month of "dangerous heat".

India and other Asian countries are stepping up preparations for what is expected to be an exceptionally severe El Niño, with governments bracing for a combination of extreme heat, heavy rainfall and food shortages.

The World Food Programme has warned that about 50 million people could be pushed into acute hunger, while UN Secretary-General António Guterres has said the phenomenon is “being supersized before our eyes”.

India, Sri Lanka focus on water and food security
In India, parts of the country have recorded a monsoon rainfall shortfall of almost 50% in September, affecting crops including rice, pulses, cotton and maize, it said. Concerns are growing over a diminished harvest and higher food prices.
The government has adopted what Agriculture Minister Shivraj Singh Chouhan described as a “protective shield for farmers”. Authorities in more than 350 vulnerable districts are strengthening water conservation and harvesting infrastructure and encouraging farmers to plant low-water, short-duration crops such as pulses and millets.
Sri Lanka is facing its worst drought in a decade, with more than 160,000 people facing drinking-water shortages as reservoirs run dry. The disaster management authorities are preparing for a situation in which freshwater supplies could disappear, potentially forcing Colombo to process seawater.

China, Taiwan step up heat preparedness
China has launched a 100-day campaign to prepare for extreme weather and protect harvests from drought and intense rainfall, it said. Beijing plans to upgrade early-warning systems and has encouraged cities to create “climate risk maps” identifying areas vulnerable to flooding and severe heat.
Taiwan held an exercise simulating three consecutive days above 40C, including scenarios involving power and water disruption, rail problems, air-conditioner failures and mass heatstroke. Its “Cool Map” platform directs vulnerable people to air-conditioned spaces.
Southeast Asia faces food pressures
Southeast Asian countries are already dealing with disrupted energy and supply chains, higher fertiliser costs and severe haze from seasonal fires. Regional rice yields are projected to fall by 8–10%.

Thiruvananthapuram, 18 September (H.S.): Kerala is likely to experience isolated heavy rainfall and thunderstorms on Friday, with the India Meteorological Department issuing a yellow alert for Alappuzha, Kottayam and Idukki districts.
The weather agency has forecast isolated rainfall ranging from 64.5 mm to 115.5 mm within 24 hours, which is classified as heavy rain. Residents in vulnerable areas have been advised to remain alert, particularly during thunderstorms and intense spells of rain.
Meanwhile, the Kerala State Disaster Management Authority has issued a ‘Kallakkadal’ warning for the coastlines of Thiruvananthapuram and Kollam districts following a forecast of unusually high waves and possible coastal flooding.
Waves ranging from 0.8 metres to 1.4 metres are expected along the Thiruvananthapuram coast, from Kappil to Pozhiyoor, and the Kollam coast, from Alappad to Edava. The warning will remain in force from 11.30 pm on Friday until 11.30 pm on Saturday.
The National Centre for Ocean Information Services has also predicted waves between 1.2 metres and 1.7 metres along the Kanyakumari coast from 8.30 pm on Friday to 11.30 am on Saturday. Fishermen and coastal residents have been urged to exercise caution because of the possibility of sea erosion and flooding in low-lying coastal areas.
A separate advisory has warned fishermen against venturing into the Andaman Sea and the southeast Bay of Bengal until September 21.
Squally winds reaching speeds of 45 kmph to 55 kmph, and occasionally touching 65 kmph, are likely over the Andaman Sea. The southeast Bay of Bengal and adjoining areas could experience winds of 40 kmph to 50 kmph, gusting up to 60 kmph.
Authorities have asked fishing vessels to avoid the affected waters during the warning period and advised coastal communities to follow official safety instructions.

title: Chilling Putin missile warning sends NATO into red alert - London Business News

Poland’s prime minister has warned that Russia could seek to test NATO’s resolve with drone or missile strikes against countries supporting Ukraine, raising concerns that the war could increasingly spill beyond the battlefield.
Donald Tusk told parliament on Thursday that intelligence assessments pointed to possible Russian attacks against NATO states, including Poland.
He said Moscow could attempt to present any resulting damage as an accident, complicating decisions over whether the alliance should respond.
The warning came after Poland scrambled military aircraft and temporarily closed airports following Russian attacks in western Ukraine close to its border. Warsaw has since increased airspace protection and rapid-response measures.
Tusk said: “We know he is plotting something bad. However, for us the most important task is to prepare for various scenarios.
“We will certainly not naively accept such messages that Russia has goodwill and will start behaving properly. There is no indication of this.”
He said intelligence from multiple sources was “very consistent and convincing”, while warning that Russia could seek to exploit uncertainty over whether an incursion was deliberate.
“There is a real risk that drones or other types of missiles could penetrate the territory of one or more countries on the eastern flank and even cause damage, while the official explanation will be that there was an accident.”
Tusk’s comments reflect growing concern among NATO members over Russian drone activity near the alliance’s eastern borders. Poland has reported a series of incidents close to its territory as Moscow has intensified attacks against western Ukraine.
The immediate concern is less about an announced Russian attack on Britain than the possibility that repeated incidents could create pressure on NATO’s collective-defence commitments. Tusk has argued that Moscow could use ostensibly accidental incursions to weaken political confidence in Article 5 and test whether member states would respond collectively.
The warnings come as NATO also presses European allies to accelerate defence investment. Secretary General Mark Rutte has called on Britain to establish a “credible path” of annual increases towards the alliance’s long-term spending target.
NATO’s own assessment is that European allies need to increase defence investment substantially as Russia rebuilds its military-industrial capacity. Rutte has said spending of roughly 3.5 per cent of GDP on core defence is required to meet the alliance’s capability targets.
Britain’s current government spending plans envisage defence expenditure reaching about 2.7 per cent of GDP by 2028-29, according to official figures, leaving a substantial gap between existing plans and the higher targets now being discussed within NATO.
The prospect of Russian missiles striking British territory would represent a far more serious escalation than the drone and reconnaissance incidents that have occurred around NATO’s eastern flank. But the intelligence warning issued by Warsaw does not establish that Russia has decided to attack the UK.
For European governments, the immediate challenge is therefore one of deterrence: strengthening air defences and military readiness while avoiding miscalculation that could turn repeated incursions into a direct confrontation between Russia and NATO.
As Russia increases its use of faster, jet-powered drones in western Ukraine, former British defence secretary Ben Wallace has described intercepting them before they cross into Nato airspace as “the next natural step”.

Producer prices rise 0.2% as heat wave lifts farm costs
Korea's producer price index rose 0.2% in August as a prolonged heat wave drove up agricultural, livestock and fisheries prices, Bank of Korea data showed.
A shopper browses fruits at a supermarket in Seoul.
NEWS1
Korea's producer prices rose in August, driven by a rise in prices of agricultural goods caused by a heat wave, central bank data showed Friday.
The producer price index, or PPI — a key gauge of future consumer inflation — increased 0.2 percent last month from a month earlier, following a 0.4 percent on-month decline, according to the preliminary data from the Bank of Korea (BOK).
In July, the index fell for the first time since August 2025.
From a year earlier, producer prices rose 7.9 percent in August, accelerating from the previous month's 7.7 percent on-month gain, the findings showed.
Producer prices are a key indicator of future inflation trends, as they influence the prices businesses charge consumers in the months ahead.
The BOK said prices of industrial goods, including petroleum and chemical products, remained flat in August compared to the previous month.
Prices of electricity, gas and water supplies gained 0.9 percent.
The data showed prices of agricultural, livestock and fisheries products rose 3.8 percent in August, accelerating from the previous month's 1.5 percent on-month rise, due to prolonged high temperatures during the month.
The domestic supply price index, which reflects both producer and import prices, dropped 1.3 percent on month in August, the data showed.
